items.title: When the map is redrawn: AI chip diversion and the bank's blind spot
items.dek: A company's revenue map can show who was billed without showing where the chips went. Banks that finance and pay for the trade face the same blind spot.
items.socialTitle: Can a bank see where the chips it finances actually go?
items.keyThesis: Banks can see the commercial and first-shipment records around AI hardware while lacking evidence of onward movement, ownership changes, or who uses the computing capacity; the control response depends on information rights and cross-functional reconciliation.

items.title: Opaque AI financing: an operational-risk deep dive
items.dek: A bank can hold a compliant supplier arrangement and still lack sight of the financing that keeps the service running. This note asks whether existing third-party rules reach that gap.
items.socialTitle: Could financing stress interrupt a bank’s critical AI service?
items.keyThesis: Third-party oversight can map the contracted service and its subcontractors while leaving visibility gaps around the financing and ownership structures that determine whether the underlying capacity remains funded.

items.title: Binance’s $6.3bn Hack: Controls Lessons for Banks
items.dek: A multi-stage compromise crossed developer endpoints, internal tooling and a container-deployment credential before reaching a wallet-signing service. The banking question is whether one compromised identity can cross the same boundaries in your environment.
items.socialTitle: Could one compromised developer reach your payment controls?
items.keyThesis: The decisive failure was the path between build credentials and a wallet-signing service: each trust boundary needs its own identity, approval and evidence.

items.title: The standard of proof
items.dek: The FCA's 19 October speech and practice review add no new AI rules — but across twenty case studies they sketch a concrete picture of the evidence supervisors may expect, on consumer outcomes, governance and operational resilience alike. For institutions already assembling parallel files for the FSB, the ECB and MAS, that evidentiary signal may matter more than any rulebook would.
items.socialTitle: What evidence will supervisors expect for AI governance?
items.keyThesis: A policy can state the standard; supervisory confidence depends on whether a firm can reconstruct evidence of outcomes, governance and resilience in practice.

items.title: No more tail risk?
items.dek: What repeated, moderate disruptions to shared dependencies mean for financial services resilience—and how firms can prepare for the next one.
items.socialTitle: What if the tail keeps coming back?
items.keyThesis: Repeated moderate outages can become a severe resilience event when shared services fail faster than firms can restore workarounds and capacity.

items.title: AI Cyber Risk: The October Escalation
items.dek: The FSB’s AI sound practices are a benchmark. The ECB’s date-certain action-plan request is a supervisory deliverable. Together with the ESRB’s sharper warning, they put a practical question to EMEA banks: are governance, response and recovery keeping pace with a faster threat?
items.socialTitle: Are AI cyber controls keeping pace with the threat?
items.keyThesis: AI cyber governance becomes operationally meaningful only when detection, containment and recovery keep pace with faster vulnerability discovery and attack preparation.

items.title: MAS, Basel and the Missing Control Layer: What AI Governance Means for EMEA Banks
items.dek: MAS’s new AI risk guidelines and its work on runtime safeguards pose a practical question for EMEA banks: can governance prove that an agent stays within its authority?
items.socialTitle: Can you prove what an AI agent is authorised to do?
items.keyThesis: Agentic governance is credible only when the firm's delegated authority, runtime safeguards and intervention rights can be evidenced in operation.

items.title: Agentic AI is moving from pilot to authority. Governance has not caught up.
items.dek: Why delegated authority, supplier assurance and a tested intervention path now matter more than another model policy.
items.socialTitle: Who can pause an AI agent?
items.keyThesis: Once an agent receives authority, governance must control its identity, scope, supplier access and interruption path throughout use—not only at model approval.

items.title: It was never about the model. It’s about the harness.
items.dek: Why the surrounding operating environment—not the model alone—determines whether AI remains governable when it enters real workflows.
items.socialTitle: The model is not the control.
items.keyThesis: The model alone does not determine operational risk; permissions, tools, data paths and the ability to intervene shape how it behaves in a real workflow.

items.title: Who owns AI risk? The micro/macroprudential split
items.dek: AI risk spans firm-level controls, market-wide vulnerabilities and the interactions between agents. What the latest regulatory signals mean for EMEA operational risk teams.
items.keyThesis: Firm-level controls and system-wide exposure sit in different mandates; effective AI risk governance needs a bridge between microprudential and macroprudential views.
